one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reveals a little-known chapter in Edsa 2's history: his role as mediator in a serious internal Vatican dispute over Cardinal Jaime Sin's activism in January 2001. He begins by establishing Sin's indispensable mobilizing capacity -- 300+ parishes and 70 parochial schools under his archbishopric, capable of producing nearly 200,000 warm bodies marching to a single drummer with their own provisions -- and his constant propeace, nonviolent exhortation. But despite this peaceableness, Sin's activism drew Vatican criticism, which surfaced silently during Edsa 2. On Jan 17, 2001, the day after the prosecutors' walkout from the Senate impeachment trial, Msgr. Socrates Villegas phoned Panganiban: Papal Nuncio Antonio Franco, on directive from his Vatican superiors, had asked Cardinal Sin to disperse the demonstrators at the Edsa Shrine. Sin refused -- preferring to resign if the Vatican insisted. To defuse the crisis, both the cardinal and the nuncio asked Panganiban, in his prior capacity as a member of the Pontifical Council for the Laity, to mediate. On Jan 18, Panganiban conferred privately with Franco and Msgr. Robinson Wijesinghe. The Vatican's two concerns were (1) whether Estrada's due process was being violated by demands for resignation without the prosecutors completing their case, and (2) whether church-state separation was being breached by clerical involvement in people power. Panganiban replied on the first point that due process presumes an objective tribunal -- and after the Senate's 11-10 refusal to open the second envelope, the bishops had seen enough to make their own evaluation; pulling the Church back at that point would plunge the nation into chaotic, bloody revolution for which the Vatican (a foreign state) could be blamed, a dismal defeat for peace and for the Church alike, since 'history is written by the victors.' On the second point, he explained that church-state separation in Philippine constitutional doctrine requires state neutrality among religious groups, not state hostility -- the Constitution's preamble itself invokes 'Almighty God,' presidential and vice-presidential oaths end with 'So help me God,' and Congress, the Cabinet, and the SC preface sessions with prayer. The state cannot fund a basilica for one sect or promote one sect's dogmas, but priests as citizens may hold public office. Doctrinally he conceded the Vatican's concern that the hierarchy should prioritize the faith and morals of the flock over secular activities, and prescribed that after Edsa 2 the Church should reexamine its position and strengthen its re-evangelizing and re-pastoring function. Franco said he would report to his superiors. Panganiban was never told what was reported, but at the Jan 20 oath-taking at the Edsa Shrine, Franco was in the front row and whispered upon seeing him: 'We have won!' He closes by noting that by Sin's 2003 retirement, the Archdiocese of Manila had been reduced to about a fourth of its original size, with five new dioceses carved out (Caloocan, Cubao, Novaliches, Parañaque, Pasig), and the low-profile conservative Gaudencio Cardinal Rosales installed in Sin's place.
